name: Old Norse
place: Iceland, Norway and the Viking world
blurb: The language of the Eddas and sagas, and the ancestor of Icelandic, Faroese, Norwegian, Danish and Swedish.
facts: Speakers called their language dǫnsk tunga, 'the Danish tongue', whether they lived in Norway, Iceland or Sweden.
English borrowed everyday words from Old Norse, among them sky, egg, knife, window, law and the pronoun they.
Most Eddic poems survive in one manuscript, the Codex Regius, written in Iceland around 1270 and returned from Copenhagen in 1971.
Someone carved runes, including the name Halfdan, into a marble balustrade of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.
Iceland's assembly, the Alþingi, first met at Þingvellir in 930. The sagas are full of its lawsuits.
Icelanders today can read the sagas with modest effort. Their language has changed remarkably little since the 1200s.

units.title: Rúnar
units.about: The sixteen runes of the Younger Futhark

guide.p: The rune row is named after its first six letters, f u þ o r k. By about AD 800 Scandinavians had cut the older 24-rune row down to these 16, the Younger Futhark.

Sixteen runes had to cover far more sounds, so each rune works hard. ᚢ writes u, o, ø, y and v. ᛁ writes i, e and j. ᛅ writes a, æ and e. ᚦ writes þ and ð. ᚴ writes k and g, ᛏ writes t and d, ᛒ writes b and p.

ᚬ first stood for a nasal a (ą) and later for o. ᛦ wrote a sound runologists spell ʀ, which grew out of an older z and mostly ends words. It later merged with ordinary r, which is why the sagas spell konungr with a plain r.

These are the long-branch forms of the great Danish runestones; quicker short-twig shapes were used too. Words were split by dots or crosses, a double letter was carved once, and an n or m before a consonant was often skipped, as in kunukʀ.

items.note: Often written R. Type it with the ʀ key.

units.title: Heill
units.about: Greet people and say who you are

guide.p: Old Norse has no indefinite article. maðr is 'man' or 'a man'.
ek em 'I am', þú ert 'you are', hann er 'he is', hon er 'she is'. Prose keeps the pronoun.
heita 'to be called' gives a name: ek heiti, þú heitir, hon heitir.

heill means 'whole, unharmed' and works as a greeting. It agrees with the person: heill to a man, heil to a woman. Óðinn walks into a giant's hall with heill þú nú, 'hail to you now' (Vafþrúðnismál 6).
þ is the th of 'thin', ð the th of 'this'. An accent marks a long vowel: á, í, ó. ǫ is an open o, as in British 'hot', and ø and œ sound like German ö.

items.note: Literally 'whole, healthy'. To a woman: heil.
From heita. þú heitir, hon heitir.

guide.p: The definite article is a suffix: -inn for masculine nouns, -in for feminine, -it for neuter. A final -a drops before it.
eigi 'not' comes straight after the verb.
For a yes-or-no question, put the verb first.
faðir, móðir, bróðir, dóttir and systir rarely take the article. faðir alone is 'father' or 'the father'.

sentences.en: she is a daughter and a sister

units.title: Í víking
units.about: Ships, the sea and the object case

guide.p: As the object of a verb, a masculine noun in -r drops it, and a feminine in -a changes it to -u. Neuter nouns stay the same. The article follows suit: víkingrinn becomes víkinginn.
Strong verbs often change their vowel in the singular. fara 'go': ek fer, þú ferr, hann ferr. koma 'come': ek kem, hann kemr. sjá 'see': ek sé, hann sér.
Endings show who does what, so the order can shift as long as the verb stays second. skipit sér konungr still means 'the king sees the ship', because konungr keeps its -r.
víkingr is the raider, víking (feminine) the raid. fara í víking, 'to go raiding', is how the sagas put it.

items.note: Motion towards home. Compare heima, 'at home'.

alt: he goes on a viking raid

units.title: Goðin
units.about: Gods, giants and the middle world

guide.p: hafa: ek hefi, þú hefir, hann hefir. gefa: ek gef, þú gefr, hann gefr. Both take the object case.
As objects, Þórr becomes Þór and Óðinn becomes Óðin.
Pronouns have object forms: ek becomes mik, þú becomes þik, hon becomes hana. hann stays hann.

An áss (plural æsir) is one of the main family of gods, led by Óðinn. The jǫtnar, giants, are their old enemies, and Miðgarðr, 'the middle enclosure', is the world of men. Snorri calls Þórr the strongest of gods and men, and Týr einhendr, one-handed, since the wolf Fenrir bit off his hand.

sentences.en: Thor is a god, not a giant

units.title: Orðstírr
units.about: Lines from the Eddas and sagas

guide.p: The 'Sayings of the High One' is Óðinn's advice poem. The first lines open with the verb: deyr is singular, deyja plural. it sama is 'the same'.
-s often marks 'of': maðr becomes manns. Hávamál 47 is about a lonely traveller who finds a friend.
Poetry can negate with a suffix -a or -at on the verb instead of eigi: var 'was', vara 'was not'. Vǫluspá 3 describes the world before creation.
ex: there was no sand nor sea

guide.p: fǫgr er hlíðin is Gunnarr in Njáls saga, chapter 75, looking back at his farm and refusing to go into exile. In chapter 70 Njáll says með lǫgum skal land várt byggja, now the motto of the Shetland Islands Council.

items.note: Literally 'word-glory': what people say of you.
A plural noun. With með: með lǫgum.

units.title: Landnám
units.about: Settlers, sagas and the past tense

guide.p: Old Norse makes the past in two ways, as English does with give, gave and call, called. Strong verbs change their vowel: gefa becomes gaf, fara fór, koma kom, vera var. Weak verbs add an ending with ð, d or t: kalla becomes kallaði, sigla sigldi, hafa hafði.
The strong past has no ending for 'I' or 'he', and -t for 'you': ek fór, þú fórt, hann fór. The plural ends in -u, often with a changed vowel: fóru, gáfu, váru, kómu.
The weak past ends in -a for 'I', -ir for 'you' and -i for 'he' or 'she': ek kallaða, þú kallaðir, hann kallaði. The plural is kǫlluðu: the u turns the a before it into ǫ.
Sagas bring in a character with the past of heita: Úlfr hét maðr, 'there was a man called Úlfr', is the first line of Egils saga, and Njáls saga opens Mǫrðr hét maðr.
ex: there was a man called Ulf

guide.p: nema land, 'to take land', is how the sources describe the settlement of Iceland from the 870s. Ari the Learned's Íslendingabók (c. 1130) names the first settler: Ingólfr hét maðr norrœnn, 'there was a Norwegian called Ingólfr'.
When a sentence opens with some other word, the verb stays in second place and the subject moves after it.

items.note: Past of sjá. Also the word for 'that' (masculine).
Past of nema. nam land: settled.

units.title: Á þingi
units.about: Whose and where: the genitive, the dative and prepositions

guide.p: Besides the nominative for the subject and the accusative for the object, Old Norse has a dative, for the one who receives and after many prepositions, and a genitive, meaning 'of' and marking the owner.
A strong masculine runs hestr, hest, hesti, hests. A neuter runs skip, skip, skipi, skips. A weak feminine like kona has konu in the other three cases. The genitive usually follows its noun.
Noun and article both change: hestrinn, hestinn, hestinum, hestsins; skipit, skipit, skipinu, skipsins; konan, konuna, konunni, konunnar.
ex: the viking was on the ship

guide.p: til 'to' takes the genitive. frá 'from' and ór 'out of' take the dative. á 'on' and í 'in' take the dative for where something is and the accusative for where it is going, so í húsinu is 'in the house' but fara í víking is 'go off raiding'. með 'with' usually takes the dative.
The dative marks who receives. Masculine nouns in -r swap it for -i: víkingi, konungi. Óðinn becomes Óðni.
ex: the king gave the viking a sword

guide.p: Each summer chieftains and farmers rode to Þingvellir for the Alþingi, the general assembly, to hear the law and settle lawsuits. ríða til þings, 'to ride to the assembly', comes up again and again in the sagas.

items.note: Dative for place, accusative for motion.
Usually takes the dative: með Óðni.
Neuter. til þings: to the assembly.
Óðinn's son, the brightest of the gods.

units.title: Vinr minn
units.about: Every pronoun, and how to say whose

guide.p: ek, mik, mér, mín; þú, þik, þér, þín; hann, hann, honum, hans; hon, hana, henni, hennar; þat, þat, því, þess. The dative is 'to' or 'for' someone.

vér is 'we' and þér 'you' to several people. 'They' is þeir for men, þær for women and þau for a mixed group. Plural verbs end in -um, -ið, -a in the present and -um, -uð, -u in the past: vér fǫrum, þeir fara; vér fórum, þeir fóru. vera is irregular: vér erum, þér eruð, þeir eru.
Old Norse kept a dual for exactly two people: vit 'we two' and þit 'you two', with object forms okkr and ykkr.
minn 'my', þinn 'your' and várr 'our' agree with their noun like adjectives and usually follow it: faðir minn, móðir mín, skip mitt.

For 'his', 'her' and 'their' use the genitive pronouns hans, hennar and þeira, unless the owner is the subject of the sentence. Then use sinn, which declines like minn. hann sá hest sinn is 'he saw his own horse'; hann sá hest hans is 'he saw his (someone else's) horse'.
Prepositions govern pronouns too: til mín 'to me' (genitive), frá honum 'from him' (dative).

items.note: To one person. Feminine þín, neuter þitt.
Points back to the subject. sín, sitt.

alt: she gave a sword to him

units.title: Ørlǫg
units.about: Shall, will and can: modal verbs and the future

guide.p: Modal verbs take a bare infinitive, which ends in -a: fara, koma, vera, ríða. There is no word for 'to'.

Most modals have a present built like a strong past, so 'he' has no ending and 'you' ends in -t: ek skal, þú skalt, hann skal 'shall, must'; ek mun, þú munt, hann mun 'will'; ek kann, þú kannt, hann kann 'know how to'; ek má, þú mátt, hann má 'may, can'. vilja 'want' has ek vil, þú vilt, hann vill.
Plurals: vér skulum, þeir skulu; munum, munu; viljum, vilja; kunnum, kunnu; megum, megu. Past: skyldi 'should', mundi 'would', vildi 'wanted', kunni 'knew how', mátti 'could'.
ex: we shall ride to the assembly

guide.p: There is no separate future tense. The present often does the job, munu says what will or is bound to happen, and skulu what someone intends or must do.

In Njáls saga 75 Gunnarr, outlawed and riding to his ship, looks back at his farm: fǫgr er hlíðin ... ok mun ek ríða heim aptr ok fara hvergi, 'and I will ride back home and go nowhere'. Staying cost him his life.
Verse moves words around freely: vin sínum skal maðr vinr vera is 'a man must be a friend to his friend'. vin sínum is dative, 'to his own friend'.

items.note: From skulu. þú skalt, vér skulum.
From vilja. ek vil, þú vilt.
From kunna. With a noun it means 'knows'.

units.title: Svá er sagt
units.about: The -sk verbs and the set phrases of saga prose

guide.p: Adding -sk to a verb turns the action back on the subject. It grew out of sik 'oneself', and later manuscripts spell it -st or -z. berja 'strike' gives berjask 'fight', hitta 'meet someone' gives hittask 'meet each other'.

Oneself: klæðask 'dress oneself'. Each other: berjask, hittask. Becoming: gerask 'become', as when Kveld-Úlfr gerðisk styggr, 'grew bad-tempered', every evening. Some verbs only appear with -sk, like óttask 'fear', and andask 'die' comes from anda 'breathe'.
The -sk takes the place of a final -r: kallar becomes kallask, berr becomes bersk. In the past it is added to the ending: hittisk, hittusk, andaðisk. With ek the old ending is -umk: ek kǫllumk.
vera with a past participle makes a passive. The participle agrees like an adjective: hann var kallaðr, hon var kǫlluð.

Saga writers pass on tradition with svá er sagt 'so it is said', and switch scenes with nú er þar til máls at taka, 'now we must take up the story at this point'. at before an infinitive is English 'to'.
A character sketch follows a pattern: hann var mikill maðr ok sterkr. Egils saga says Úlfr was svá mikill ok sterkr at eigi váru hans jafningjar, 'so big and strong that there were none his equal'.

units.title: Skáldskapr
units.about: Kennings, Eddic metre and saga dialogue

guide.p: A kenning names something with a riddle: a base word plus a genitive. Ymis hauss 'Ymir's skull' is the sky, Ymis blóð 'Ymir's blood' the sea, haddr Sifjar 'Sif's hair' gold, Kvasis blóð 'Kvasir's blood' poetry. Snorri collected hundreds in Skáldskaparmál for young poets.

Grímnismál 40 tells how the gods built the world from the giant Ymir: ór Ymis holdi var jǫrð of skǫpuð ... en ór hausi himinn. of is a filler word poets used to fill out a line, and the second half leaves out its verb.
ex: and from the skull the sky

guide.p: Poets also used heiti, poetic names. Gylfaginning 20 explains two of Óðinn's: Alfǫðr 'all-father', because he is father of all the gods, and Valfǫðr 'father of the slain', because all who fall in battle are his adopted sons. ok here means 'also'.

fornyrðislag, 'old-lore metre', pairs short lines of two stresses each, tied by alliteration, as in Vǫluspá: Sól tér sortna, / sígr fold í mar. Hávamál uses ljóðaháttr, 'song metre': two short lines, then a full line that stands alone, as in deyr fé, / deyja frændr, / deyr sjálfr it sama. Stanza 77 ends with the one thing that never dies: dómr um dauðan hvern.

Saga speech is short and understated. In Njáls saga 77 Gunnarr's bowstring is cut while he holds off his attackers. He asks his wife Hallgerðr for two locks of her hair, and when she asks whether anything depends on it he says only líf mitt liggr við. She refuses, to repay an old slap. fá is a command, 'give!': the command form is the bare stem, as in far! 'go!' and kom! 'come!'.

-st and -ast make superlatives: verst 'worst', mest 'most', beztr 'best'. At the end of Laxdæla saga (ch. 78) Guðrún's son asks which of her four husbands she loved most. She answers þeim var ek verst er ek unna mest, using unna 'love'.
